source.title: Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak

page_placements.theme: Early signals and commitment windows support safety monitoring
Recovery after compliant openings is model- and prefix-dependent
Activation interventions control refusal with variable dimensionality

record.tranche_reason: The study tests prefill-induced refusal failure and response-position dependence with behavioral and causal activation interventions, rather than reproducing the original per-token KL measurement or fine-tuning procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper tests affirmative response prefills and the response-site mechanisms they engage. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, suffix or decoding attacks as independent bypass methods, or training intended to deepen safety. Several discussion and appendix claims about other attacks are cited or scoped rather than evaluated as refusal-rate results here.
record.test_reason: The study measures how far affirmative response prefills reduce harmful-prompt refusal in six instruct models (V4). It also ablates attention heads and layers to look for a compact refusal circuit (V5). It uses different methods from the originals: no fine-tuning and no aligned-vs-base per-token KL.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a prefill makes aligned models comply while the prompt-side harm representation stays intact. The failure is localized to an early response window, and its grip is largely generic autoregressive conditioning, with a small safety-specific refusal pull. Refusal has no compact internal handle across the tested directions, subspaces, layers and heads. As a practical consequence, a prompt-side monitor is immune to response-site attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses affirmative prefills and causal activation/attention interventions to locate the response-site failure. It does not reproduce harmful/benign fine-tuning or the aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The prefill effect is weaker on Qwen2.5-7B than on the smaller instruct models. Response-site restoration varies with position and intervention strength: the first half is effective, the second half nearly inert, and halving the per-position coefficient can eliminate the effect. A temperature 0.7 check retains the prefill refusal collapse but weakens harm-direction restoration. Prefill length/commitment also changes restoration magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: The prefill's grip is localized to an early multi-token response window, not the onset token alone. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, harm-direction injection over the first half restores 42% vs 41% for the whole response and 6% for the second half; refuse-state transfer restores 74%. Knocking out early attention to the prefill restores 24% vs 1% for the matched control. Phi-3-mini replicates these.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant control under prefill attacks is concentrated in an early multi-token response window, measured causally rather than by KL (a causal analogue of V3).

fits_no_version.finding: The refuse/comply decision is decodable by a full probe (~0.85) but not by any single direction (≤0.73), and steering that direction does nothing. SmolLM2 is a counterexample.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal decision is distributed across activation directions rather than carried by one direction.

fits_no_version.finding: In base models with no safety tuning, early prefill-attention knockout cuts harmful continuation by a similar amount (64→25% at 1.5B, 68→30% at 7B). The prefill's grip is therefore generic autoregressive conditioning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefill dependence is generic conditioning, with a small safety-specific refusal attractor on top.

record.problems: The core mechanism battery is limited to two instruct models, with per-condition sample sizes varying. The larger-scale behavioral refusal effect is weaker at 7B, and frontier scale is untested. The paper identifies MLP neurons and SAE features as untested for compact safety mechanisms. Some reported grid maxima are post-selection; the study notes this and settles selected effects with fixed-cell tests. The full-attention-ablation refusal-string result is confounded by gibberish generation.
record.rows_left_out: No targeted claim-relevant results omitted under the 60-row limit. Fine-tuning results, per-token KL values, and training-to-deepen-safety results are absent from this study rather than omitted.

untested.parts: Adversarial suffixes and decoding-parameter attacks are not evaluated as bypass methods. Only affirmative prefills, plus a temperature-0.7 check, are tested.
No weight pruning or low-rank localization, as in the original safety-critical-weights framing. MLP neurons and SAE features are untested. Only attention heads and layers are ablated, in two models.
No manipulation of training data or objective.

missing.what: On 24 dual-use intent triplets, the prefill drops refusal from 100% to 0% on bare prompts read as harmful-intent (62% to 0% over all 24); one model.
At temperature 0.7, plain refusal stays at 100% and the attack strips it to 0% (n=40), so the bypass is not a greedy artifact.
Short prefill 'Sure,' vs a long committal prefill: restoration magnitude depends on prefill length and commitment. This varies the attack setting.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r8–r16 were relinked from V4 to none. They measure mechanism and restoration, not the bypass rate; they are kept under fits_no_version as a causal, positional analogue of V3. V5 is judged only from component ablations, because the direction and probe rows concern activation space, not weights or ranks. The study cites Qi et al. (an original source) but is not itself an original.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or example-count sweep.
No benign-data fine-tuning or benign-data selection experiment.
No measurement of per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models. The paper tests response-position effects causally, which is not the KL measurement named in this version.
Tests affirmative prefills and some interventions that disrupt prefill dependence. Does not independently test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes as bypass methods.
Tests selected directions, attention heads and layers, and ablation/steering behavior. MLP neurons and SAE features remain untested; the paper notes these and frontier scale as open.
No controlled change to safety-training data or objective to test what produces shallowness.
No training intervention designed to deepen safety and no test of whether such deepening holds up.

reader_labels.reason: Early-window counter-signals restore refusal, whereas second-half harm-direction addition is nearly inert; this supports an early response-site locus but not a claim that the onset token alone is the whole mechanism; see r8–r13.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Removing early attention to prefill keys partially restores refusal (0.03 to 0.24), while matched and late-window controls do not; the paper attributes the prefill grip principally to generic conditioning, not a complete safety-specific bypass mechanism; see r14–r16.

reader_labels.reason: Individual heads and most tested layers do not selectively remove refusal; broad ablation that yields zero refusal also yields gibberish, while the 14B input-layer change is partial and not selective; see r17–r20.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: A single direction reads the decision less well than the full probe and steering that direction does not restore refusal, consistent with a distributed rather than compact single-direction computation; see r21–r23.
